questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are true with respect to the interaction of a web browser with a web server using HTTP 1.1?
options: HTTP 1.1 facilitates downloading multiple objects of the same webpage over the same TCP connection, if the objects are stored in the same server
HTTP 1.1 facilitates downloading multiple objects of the same webpage over the same TCP connection, even if they are stored in different servers
HTTP 1.1 facilitates sending a request for downloading one object without waiting for a previously requested object to be downloaded completely
HTTP 1.1 facilitates downloading multiple webpages on the same server to be downloaded over a single TCP connection

steps.title: Definitions and the deciding rule
steps.body: HTTP is the request-response protocol a browser uses to fetch web objects (the HTML file, each image, each script). It runs over TCP. A TCP connection joins exactly two endpoints: the browser and one server. In HTTP 1.0 each object used a new connection (non-persistent). HTTP 1.1 made connections persistent by default: after the response, the connection stays open for further requests to the same server. HTTP 1.1 also allows pipelining: the browser may send the next request before the previous response has fully arrived. Rule: judge each statement by asking whether it needs a connection to more than one server, or whether it reuses one connection with one server.

steps.title: Statement A
steps.body: Objects on the same server can all travel on one persistent connection. True.

steps.title: Statement B
steps.body: A connection ends at one server. An object stored on a different server needs a separate connection to that server. False.

steps.title: Statements C and D
steps.body: C describes pipelining: the next request is sent without waiting for the earlier response to finish. True. D: a persistent connection is tied to the server, not to a page, so later pages from the same server reuse it. True. The answer is A, C and D.

shortcut.body: Persistent connection = one TCP connection per server, reused for any number of requests, pages included. Only the claim that crosses servers (B) fails. Safe, because TCP always ends at a single server.

traps.text: Choosing B: a connection cannot be shared between two different servers, however persistent it is.
Dropping D because persistence is thought to last for one page only: the connection is per server, so it carries several pages.
Dropping C because pipelining is thought to be an HTTP/2 feature: HTTP 1.1 defines it too, though browsers rarely enable it.

recognize.clues: The words HTTP 1.1, same TCP connection and without waiting for a previously requested object point to persistent connections and pipelining. The options differ in which server holds the objects and what stays open.
recognize.contrast: HTTP/2 multiplexing is a different feature: pipelining in HTTP 1.1 sends requests early, but the responses still come back in request order.

check.body: Test every statement against the one fixed fact that a TCP connection ends at a single server. Only the statement that names a second server on the same connection contradicts it. The other three each stay within one server, so none of them breaks that fact.

sources.label: GATE 2026 CS-1 answer key, IIT Guwahati (organising institute)

hints.text: For each statement, ask how many servers the browser must talk to and how many TCP connections that takes.
Recall what a persistent connection is, and what HTTP 1.0 did differently for every object.
A TCP connection has exactly two ends, so whatever a statement claims must fit one browser and one server on that connection.
Sort the statements into those that reuse a connection with one server and those that need a second server, and note separately which one is about not waiting for a reply.

variation.stem: Which of the following statements is/are true about a browser using HTTP 1.1 with a server?
options: A persistent connection to a server can carry the requests for an HTML file and for the images stored on that same server
A single TCP connection can carry requests to two different servers, because HTTP 1.1 connections are persistent
With pipelining, the browser may send its next request before the response to the previous request is complete
The server must close the TCP connection after every response, as HTTP 1.1 connections are non-persistent by default
variation.explanation: A TCP connection joins one browser to one server, so reuse works across objects of that server only. That makes the first statement true and the second false. Pipelining is allowed in HTTP 1.1, so the third is true. HTTP 1.1 connections are persistent by default, so the fourth is false.

questions.stem:
A user starts browsing a webpage hosted at a remote server. The browser opens a single TCP connection to fetch the entire webpage from the server. The webpage consists of a top-level index page with multiple embedded image objects. Assume that all caches (e.g., DNS cache, browser cache) are all initially empty. The following packets leave the user's computer in some order.
(i) HTTP GET request for the index page
(ii) DNS request to resolve the web server's name to its IP address
(iii) HTTP GET request for an image object
(iv) TCP SYN to open a connection to the web server
Which one of the following is the CORRECT chronological order (earliest in time to latest) of the packets leaving the computer ?
options: (iv), (ii), (iii), (i)
(ii), (iv), (iii), (i)
(ii), (iv), (i), (iii)
(iv), (ii), (i), (iii)

steps.title: Definitions and the deciding rule
steps.body: DNS (Domain Name System) turns a server name into an IP address. TCP SYN is the first packet of the TCP handshake that opens a connection. An HTTP GET asks the server for an object. Rule: a packet cannot leave before the thing it needs exists. Each step needs the result of the one before.

steps.title: Order the dependencies
steps.body: SYN is sent to an IP address, which the empty DNS cache does not have, so DNS (ii) comes before SYN (iv). A GET goes over an open connection, so SYN (iv) comes before both GETs. The image names appear only inside the index page, so the index GET (i) comes before the image GET (iii).

steps.title: Result
steps.body: The only order is (ii), (iv), (i), (iii), which is option C. A script that tries all 24 orders under these four constraints leaves exactly this one.

shortcut.body: Name, then connection, then page, then page contents: DNS, SYN, index, image. Scan the options for the one that starts with (ii) and ends with (iii).

traps.text: SYN first and image GET before index GET: ignores that the IP address comes from DNS and that the images are discovered from the index page.
DNS and SYN correct, but the image is requested before the index: nobody knows the image URL until the index arrives.
SYN before DNS: a connection needs the IP address, which DNS supplies.

recognize.clues: Empty caches, a single TCP connection and an index page with embedded images fix a chain: look up the name, open the connection, fetch the page, then fetch what the page references.
recognize.contrast: A page-load time question in http-timing counts round trips; this one asks only for the order of packets, not for elapsed time.

check.body: Try breaking the chosen order. Putting the SYN before the DNS request leaves no address to connect to, and putting the image request before the index request leaves no image name to ask for. Every swap violates a dependency, so the order is forced.

solutionDiagram.alt: Sequence of packets from the browser: DNS request, TCP SYN, GET index, GET image

sources.label: GATE 2024 CS1 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: Which of these packets needs something that another packet in the list produces first?
Recall what each protocol delivers: DNS gives an address, SYN opens a connection, GET asks for an object.
A packet can leave only after the thing it depends on exists, so order the packets by dependency and not by guess.
Draw an arrow from each packet to the packets that need its result, take the one with no incoming arrow, and repeat.
With every cache empty, the very first packet out of the computer is the one that finds the server address.

variation.stem:
A browser with empty caches opens one TCP connection to a server to load a page. The page is an index file that references one script file; the browser closes the connection once the script has arrived. The following packets leave the computer in some order.
(i) TCP FIN to close the connection
(ii) HTTP GET for the script file
(iii) DNS request for the server name
(iv) HTTP GET for the index page
(v) TCP SYN to the server
Which one is the correct chronological order, earliest first?
variation.explanation: Chain the dependencies: the name lookup (iii) gives the address, the SYN (v) needs that address, the index GET (iv) needs the open connection, the script GET (ii) needs the script name found in the index, and the FIN (i) comes after the last object. Only (iii), (v), (iv), (ii), (i) satisfies all four links; the other options swap the lookup and SYN, the index and script requests, or close the connection too early.

questions.stem:
Suppose in a web browser, you click on the www.gate-2023.in URL. The browser cache is empty. The IP address for this URL is not cached in your local host, so a DNS lookup is triggered (by the local DNS server deployed on your local host) over the 3-tier DNS hierarchy in an iterative mode. No resource records are cached anywhere across all DNS servers.
Let RTT denote the round trip time between your local host and DNS servers in the DNS hierarchy. The round trip time between the local host and the web server hosting www.gate-2023.in is also equal to RTT. The HTML file associated with the URL is small enough to have negligible transmission time and negligible rendering time by your web browser, which references 10 equally small objects on the same web server.
Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT about the minimum elapsed time between clicking on the URL and your browser fully rendering it?
options: 7 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
5 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.
9 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
6 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.

steps.title: Definitions and the deciding rule
steps.body: RTT is the time for a small packet to go to a host and come back. Iterative DNS: the asker visits each server in turn, and each visit costs one RTT. Opening a TCP connection costs 1 RTT (the handshake), and an HTTP request with its response costs 1 RTT. Non-persistent HTTP opens a new connection for every object. Persistent HTTP reuses one connection. Pipelining sends all requests back to back without waiting. Transmission times are zero, so only RTTs count.

steps.title: DNS part
steps.body: A 3-tier hierarchy is root, top-level domain, authoritative. Three servers are asked one after another: 3 RTT.

steps.title: Non-persistent, 5 parallel connections
steps.body: The HTML file needs a handshake (1) and a request (1) = 2 RTT. Then 10 objects go 5 at a time: 2 rounds, each a handshake plus a request = 2 RTT, so 4 RTT. Total 3 + 2 + 4 = 9 RTT. Option C is true, option A is false.

steps.title: Persistent with pipelining
steps.body: After DNS (3) comes one handshake (1), the HTML request (1), and then all 10 object requests sent together, answered in 1 RTT. Total 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 RTT. Option D is true, option B is false.

shortcut.body: DNS = 3 always. Persistent pipelined = 3 + 1 (TCP) + 1 (HTML) + 1 (all objects) = 6. Non-persistent with k parallel = 3 + 2 + 2 x ceil(10/k) = 9. Unsafe if the question says serial requests or non-negligible transmission time.

traps.text: 7 RTT: counts only one round of parallel objects, or forgets the handshake in the object round.

5 RTT: omits one of the 1-RTT terms, either the TCP handshake or the single pipelined round for the 10 objects (3+1+1). Both are needed: the connection must be opened first, and the objects are fetched only after the HTML arrives.
Counting 2 RTT for DNS instead of 3 by skipping the authoritative server.
Treating the HTML fetch as part of the 5 parallel connections: the objects are unknown until the HTML arrives.

recognize.clues: Negligible transmission and rendering times, time measured in RTT, and a count of embedded objects fetched either in parallel or with pipelining signal a sum of round trips.
recognize.contrast: The persistence topic only asks how many connections are needed. Here the same facts must become elapsed time, so the DNS and handshake round trips count too.

check.body: Check against a bound. Even with unlimited parallel non-persistent connections, the object phase is one handshake plus one request, 2 RTT, giving 3 + 2 + 2 = 7. Five connections cannot beat unlimited ones, and they need two such rounds, so the total is 7 + 2 = 9.

solutionDiagram.alt: Timeline in RTTs: three DNS RTTs, TCP handshake, HTML request, one pipelined round for 10 objects, 6 in total

sources.label: GATE 2023 CS answer key, IIT Kanpur (organising institute, PDF author IITK_GATE), IIT Guwahati archive copy

hints.text: What costs one round trip in this setup, and what costs nothing because transmission and rendering are negligible?
Recall the cost in round trips of an iterative DNS lookup, a TCP handshake and one HTTP request with its response.
The object requests cannot start until the HTML file has arrived, because the object names are inside it.
Write the total as DNS rounds, plus the HTML fetch, plus the rounds the 10 objects need, once for each connection mode; parallel connections give a ceiling of objects over connections.
The DNS lookup over three tiers is the same number of round trips in both modes, so add it first and then add the HTML fetch with its connection.

variation.stem: A browser fetches a page from www.example.test with an empty browser cache and no cached DNS records. The name is resolved iteratively over a 4-tier DNS hierarchy, and every DNS server and the web server are one RTT away from the local host. The HTML file and the 8 small objects it references have negligible transmission and rendering time, and all objects are on the same web server. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT about the minimum elapsed time before the page is fully rendered?
options: 9 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 4 parallel TCP connections.
10 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 4 parallel TCP connections.
6 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.
7 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.
variation.explanation: DNS costs 4 RTT in either mode. Non-persistent with 4 connections: the HTML needs 2 RTT, then ceil(8/4) = 2 rounds of 2 RTT, so 4 + 2 + 4 = 10. Persistent with pipelining: 4 + 1 (handshake) + 1 (HTML) + 1 (all objects together) = 7. The neighbouring options each drop or add one RTT term.

questions.stem: Consider the resolution of the domain name www.gate.org.in by a DNS resolver. Assume that no resource records are cached anywhere across the DNS servers and that iterative query mechanism is used in the resolution. The number of DNS query-response pairs involved in completely resolving the domain name is _____________.

steps.title: Definitions and the deciding rule
steps.body: A domain name is read right to left: in, then org, then gate, then www. A DNS server is responsible for one zone and knows the servers one level below it. In iterative resolution, the resolver itself asks each server in turn; a server that cannot answer replies with a referral to the next server. Each request plus its reply is one query-response pair. Rule: one pair per server consulted, and with empty caches the walk starts at a root server.

steps.title: Walk the names
steps.body: Pair 1: root server, refers to the .in servers. Pair 2: the .in server, refers to the org.in servers. Pair 3: the org.in server, refers to the gate.org.in servers. Pair 4: the gate.org.in server, which stores www and returns its IP address.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: The resolution takes 4 query-response pairs in total.

shortcut.body: Count the dots in the name: 3 dots means 3 referrals plus the final answer, 4 pairs; equivalently root plus one server per label to the left of www. Unsafe if the question says a name server is recursive or has caches.

traps.text: 3: counting only root, .in and gate.org.in, skipping the org.in level that the name shows.
5: adding a pair for the local resolver or for the web server itself; the HTTP fetch is not a DNS pair.

recognize.clues: The words iterative, no records cached and query-response pairs tell you to walk from the root down, one server per level.
recognize.contrast: In recursive resolution the resolver sends a single query and the server contacted does the walk, so the resolver sees one pair, not the length of the walk.

check.body: Count by labels. The name has four labels (in, org, gate, www), and the walk takes one pair per label, ending at the server that knows www. Dropping www would leave three pairs, matching the three referrals before the final answer.

solutionDiagram.alt: Resolver queries root, .in, org.in and gate.org.in in turn; the last returns the IP address

sources.label: GATE 2022 CS answer key, IIT Kharagpur (organising institute, named in the page banner), IIT Guwahati archive copy

hints.text: Which servers must the resolver contact, and in what order, when it starts with nothing cached?
Recall how a domain name splits into labels and which server is responsible for each level.
In iterative resolution every server consulted gives one query-response pair, either a referral or the final address.
List the labels from the right, mark which server answers for each, and note which one finally holds the host name.

variation.stem: Consider the resolution of the domain name www.cs.uni.ac.in by a DNS resolver. Assume no resource records are cached anywhere, that iterative querying is used, and that the name servers for in, ac.in, uni.ac.in and cs.uni.ac.in are all different, the last one holding the address of www. The number of DNS query-response pairs needed to resolve the name completely is _____________.
variation.explanation: Start at a root server, which refers the resolver to the in servers. Then ac.in, then uni.ac.in, then cs.uni.ac.in each answer once, the last returning the address of www. That is one pair per label, 5 in all.

questions.stem: Assume that you have made a request for a web page through your web browser to a web server. Initially the browser cache is empty. Further, the browser is configured to send HTTP requests in non-persistent mode. The web page contains text and five very small images. The minimum number of TCP connections required to display the web page completely in your browser is _____________.

steps.title: Definitions and the deciding rule
steps.body: A web page is a base HTML file plus the objects it references (here five images). HTTP runs over TCP. In non-persistent mode the server closes the connection after sending one object, so every object needs its own TCP connection. Rule: connections = number of objects fetched.

steps.title: Count objects
steps.body: The empty cache means nothing is reused: 1 HTML file (the text) + 5 images = 6 objects.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: 6 connections. Opening them in parallel changes the time, not the count.

shortcut.body: Non-persistent: connections = 1 + number of embedded objects = 6. Persistent mode would need 1.

traps.text: 5: forgetting that the HTML text itself needs a connection.
1: assuming a persistent connection, which the question rules out.
2: assuming one connection for the text and one shared by the images.

recognize.clues: The phrases non-persistent mode, text and five very small images, and number of TCP connections ask for connections per object.
recognize.contrast: Persistent mode would reuse one connection, and a page-load time question in http-timing would ask for time rather than a count.

check.body: Test the formula on a page with no images: it still needs one connection for the text, so the count is the number of images plus one. With five images that gives 6, and the question rules out the persistent case that would give 1.

sources.label: GATE 2020 CS answer key, IIT Delhi (organising institute), print of its paper-and-key web page, IIT Guwahati archive

hints.text: How many separate things must the browser download before the page can be displayed?
Recall what non-persistent HTTP does with the TCP connection after each response.
In non-persistent mode, one connection is used for every object the browser fetches.
List the objects: the file that holds the text and each embedded item, then match each to a connection.

variation.stem: A browser with an empty cache is set to non-persistent HTTP. A page consists of one HTML file, one style sheet and seven small images, two of which are stored on a second server. The minimum number of TCP connections needed to display the page completely is _____________.
variation.explanation: Non-persistent HTTP uses one connection per object, whichever server holds it. The objects are 1 HTML file, 1 style sheet and 7 images, so 1 + 1 + 7 = 9 connections; the second server changes where some connections go, not how many there are.

questions.stem: Which of the following protocol pairs can be used to send and retrieve e-mails (in that order)?
options: IMAP, POP3
SMTP, POP3
SMTP, MIME
IMAP, SMTP

steps.title: Definitions and the deciding rule
steps.body: E-mail has two directions. Sending moves a message from the user's mail client to a mail server and between mail servers: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) does this, by pushing. Retrieving lets a user pull stored mail from a mailbox server: POP3 (download, usually deleting from server) and IMAP (read and manage mail on the server) do this. MIME is not a transfer protocol; it is a format for non-text content such as attachments. Rule: pair a sending protocol first with a retrieval protocol second.

steps.title: Check each option
steps.body: A: IMAP retrieves, so it cannot be first. B: SMTP sends, POP3 retrieves. C: MIME is a format, not a retrieval protocol. D: IMAP retrieves, so it cannot be first, and SMTP cannot retrieve.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: The pair that sends first and retrieves second is SMTP, POP3, which is option B.

shortcut.body: Only SMTP sends. Find the option whose first entry is SMTP, then rule out MIME as a protocol. Safe for any send-then-retrieve question.

traps.text: Both are retrieval protocols; neither sends.
MIME describes message content; it cannot retrieve mail.
Reversed order: IMAP retrieves and SMTP sends.

recognize.clues: The wording send and retrieve (in that order) asks for one protocol per direction, chosen from SMTP, POP3, IMAP and MIME.
recognize.contrast: POP3 and IMAP both retrieve: IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs it, while POP3 usually downloads it. MIME is a content format and moves no mail.

check.body: Eliminate by role. Any option whose first entry cannot send is out, and any option containing MIME is out because MIME carries no mail across the network. Each option but one fails at least one of these two tests.

sources.label: GATE 2019 CS final answer key (organised by IIT Madras), gateexam.info copy

hints.text: Which protocol pushes mail toward a server, and which ones pull it from a mailbox?
Recall the job of SMTP, POP3, IMAP and MIME in handling e-mail.
A valid pair names a sending protocol first and a retrieval protocol second, and each entry must be a protocol that moves mail.
Mark each protocol as sends, retrieves or neither, then check each option for the right order.

variation.stem: A mail client first reads messages kept in a mailbox on the server, and later submits a new message for delivery. Which of the following protocol pairs can be used for these two actions (in that order)?
options: SMTP, IMAP
IMAP, MIME
IMAP, SMTP
POP3, IMAP
variation.explanation: Reading stored mail is retrieval (POP3 or IMAP); submitting a message for delivery is sending (SMTP). The retrieval protocol must come first. Pairs that start with SMTP or that put the retrieval protocol second fail, and MIME is a content format, not a transfer protocol.
